title: Merging Two Sorted Linked Lists

phrases.explanation: Arranged from smallest to largest value
Visit each node in the linked list one by one from head to tail
An unusual or extreme input scenario that needs special handling
Keep a reference variable that tracks a specific position in the data structure
Performing the task without allocating significant extra memory

concept: Given two sorted linked lists, merge them into a single linked list that is also sorted. Return the head of the merged list.

solutions.label: Collect and Sort
solutions.summary: Collect all values from both lists into an array, sort the array, then build a new linked list from the sorted values.

solutions.label: Iterative Merge with Dummy Node
solutions.summary: Use a dummy node and a tail pointer. Compare nodes from both lists one by one, appending the smaller node to the merged list.

solutions.label: Recursive Merge
solutions.summary: Recursively choose the smaller head node and set its next pointer to the result of merging the remaining nodes.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.diagram:
graph TD
    subgraph List1["List 1"]
        A1["1"]:::red --> A2["3"]:::red --> A3["5"]:::red
    end
    subgraph List2["List 2"]
        B1["2"]:::red --> B2["4"]:::red --> B3["6"]:::red
    end
    A3 --> R["? Merged Result"]
    B3 --> R
    R --> M1["1"] --> M2["2"] --> M3["3"] --> M4["4"] --> M5["5"] --> M6["6"]
    classDef red fill:#f87171,stroke:#333,color:#fff

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: Here is today's problem. You are given two linked lists, and each one is already sorted in ascending order. Your task is to merge them into a single sorted linked list and return its head.

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: Got it. So both input lists are sorted from smallest to largest. Can I ask a few clarifying questions? What types of values do the nodes contain, and how large can the lists be?

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: Each node holds an integer. Each list can have between zero and fifty nodes, and node values range from negative fifty to fifty.

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: What if one or both lists are empty? And should I create new nodes or reuse the existing ones?

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: If a list is empty, just return the other list. You may reuse existing nodes. No need to create new ones.

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: Understood. So given list one as 1, 3, 5 and list two as 2, 4, 6, the result should be 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6. Let me think about approaches.

sections.title: Collect and Sort
sections.diagram:
graph TD
    subgraph Step1["Step 1: Collect All Values"]
        L1["List1: 1→3→5"]:::blue --> Arr["Array: 1, 3, 5, 2, 4, 6"]
        L2["List2: 2→4→6"]:::blue --> Arr
    end
    subgraph Step2["Step 2: Sort Array"]
        Arr --> Sorted["Sorted: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6"]:::blue
    end
    subgraph Step3["Step 3: Build New List"]
        Sorted --> N1["1"]:::blue --> N2["2"]:::blue --> N3["3"]:::blue --> N4["4"]:::blue --> N5["5"]:::blue --> N6["6"]:::blue
    end
    classDef blue fill:#60a5fa,stroke:#333,color:#fff

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: My first idea is straightforward. I traverse both lists and collect all values into an array. Then I sort the array and build a new linked list from those sorted values.

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: That works. Can you walk through the example?

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: Sure. From list one I get 1, 3, 5, and from list two I get 2, 4, 6. The combined array is 1, 3, 5, 2, 4, 6. After sorting, it becomes 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6. Then I build a linked list from that.

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: What is the time complexity?

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: Let n be the total number of nodes in both lists. Collecting takes O of n, sorting takes O of n log n, and building the list takes O of n. So overall it is O of n log n time and O of n space for the array.

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: That is correct, but we are ignoring the fact that both lists are already sorted. Can you do better?

sections.title: Iterative Merge with Dummy Node
sections.diagram:
graph TD
    D["Dummy Node"]:::purple --> N1["1 ← from L1"]:::purple
    N1 --> N2["2 ← from L2"]:::purple
    N2 --> N3["3 ← from L1"]:::purple
    N3 --> N4["4 ← from L2"]:::purple
    N4 --> N5["5 ← from L1"]:::purple
    N5 --> N6["6 ← from L2"]:::purple
    N6 --> End["null"]
    classDef purple fill:#a78bfa,stroke:#333,color:#fff

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: Since both lists are already sorted, I can use two pointers. I create a dummy node and a tail pointer. At each step, I compare the current nodes of both lists and attach the smaller one to tail, then advance that pointer.

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: Walk me through it with our example.

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: I start with list one pointing at 1 and list two pointing at 2. I compare: 1 is smaller, so I attach it to tail and advance list one to 3. Next, 2 is smaller than 3, so I attach 2 and advance list two to 4. I keep comparing: 3 then 4 then 5 then 6. When one list is exhausted, I attach the remainder of the other list directly.

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: What about complexity?

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: Each node is visited exactly once, so the time complexity is O of n where n is the total number of nodes. The space complexity is O of 1 since I only use a dummy node and a tail pointer, no extra data structures.

sections.title: Recursive Merge
sections.diagram:
graph TD
    Call1["merge(1→3→5, 2→4→6)"]:::orange --> Pick1["Pick 1, recurse"]
    Pick1 --> Call2["merge(3→5, 2→4→6)"]:::orange --> Pick2["Pick 2, recurse"]
    Pick2 --> Call3["merge(3→5, 4→6)"]:::orange --> Pick3["Pick 3, recurse"]
    Pick3 --> Call4["merge(5, 4→6)"]:::orange --> Pick4["Pick 4, recurse"]
    Pick4 --> Call5["merge(5, 6)"]:::orange --> Pick5["Pick 5, recurse"]
    Pick5 --> Call6["merge(null, 6)"]:::orange --> Pick6["Return 6"]
    classDef orange fill:#fb923c,stroke:#333,color:#fff

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: There is also a recursive approach. At each call, I compare the heads of both lists. The smaller head becomes the current node, and its next pointer is set to the result of recursively merging the rest.

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: How does the recursion unfold with our example?

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: First call compares 1 and 2. Pick 1, then recurse with 3, 5 and 2, 4, 6. Next, pick 2, recurse with 3, 5 and 4, 6. Then pick 3, pick 4, pick 5, and finally the base case returns 6. The chain builds up as the recursion unwinds.

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: What about the complexity here?

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: Time complexity is still O of n since we process each node once. But space complexity is O of n due to the recursion call stack. So while elegant, the iterative approach is better for space.

sections.title: Summary
sections.diagram:
graph LR
    subgraph Comparison["Approach Comparison"]
        BF["Collect and Sort\nTime: O of n log n\nSpace: O of n"]:::blue
        IT["Iterative Merge\nTime: O of n\nSpace: O of 1"]:::purple
        RC["Recursive Merge\nTime: O of n\nSpace: O of n"]:::orange
    end
    BF --> IT --> RC
    classDef blue fill:#60a5fa,stroke:#333,color:#fff
    classDef purple fill:#a78bfa,stroke:#333,color:#fff
    classDef orange fill:#fb923c,stroke:#333,color:#fff

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: Nice work. Let us recap. The brute force collects and sorts all values in O of n log n time. The iterative merge with a dummy node runs in O of n time and O of 1 space, making it the most efficient. The recursive merge is also O of n time but uses O of n stack space.

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: Right. In an interview, I would go with the iterative approach since it has the best overall complexity. The key insight is to leverage the fact that both lists are already sorted by comparing heads one step at a time.

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: Exactly. The dummy node technique is a pattern that comes up often in linked list problems. Great job.
